title: "Foreign Influence by Authoritarian Governments: Introducing New Data and Evidence"
# subtitle: Explore the data using our [Shiny apps](https://web.sas.upenn.edu/mlp-devlab/rai/) 
abstract: Policymakers are increasingly concerned about the revival of superpower conflict, which is particularly evident in Russia’s and China’s intensifying efforts to influence less powerful nations. To date, the absence of quantitative data has limited systematic investigation of this resurgence of authoritarian influence activity. We introduce a new country-month dataset tracking reports of Russian and Chinese influence across 66 low- and middle-income countries from 2012 through August 2025. We construct the data using large language models applied to an original corpus of over 120 million articles from high-quality domestic news sources. We use these data to describe temporal and cross-national trends in influence activity. As a test case, we examine Russian activity prior to the invasion of Ukraine, documenting a dramatic and previously undetected surge in diplomacy and hard power reporting across countries. These findings demonstrate the dataset’s value for both theory testing and foreign policy analysis.
# ORIGINAL ABSTRACT: Policymakers are increasingly concerned about the revival of superpower conflict. Increased competition among great powers has been especially evident in the exercise of foreign influence, where Russia and China have increased their efforts to influence less powerful nations. To date, the absence of quantitative data has limited systematic investigation of this resurgence of authoritarian influence activity. We introduce a new, country-month dataset tracking reports of influence by Russia and China in 66 aid-receiving low- and middle-income countries from 2012 through August 2025. We construct the data by applying large language models (LLMs) to an original corpus of more than 120 million news articles sourced from high-quality, domestic news sources and use it to describe trends in influence activity over time and across countries. Finally, as a test case, use the data to examine Russian influence activity in the months before the invasion of Ukraine. We document a dramatic, previously undetected, pre-invasion surge in diplomacy and hard power reporting across many countries. In doing so, we show that this data is useful for both theory testing and foreign policy decision-making.

## Introduction

The last 15 years have seen Russia and China become both more autocratic
and more assertive in their foreign policies [@diamond2020democratic]. Both have 
increased efforts to influence less powerful nations and secure strategic partnerships. 
Scholars and policymakers have voiced growing concerns about a resurgence of 
authoritarian influence, driving high-level foreign policy decisions and major 
investments by Western governments in strengthening ties with strategically 
important countries.

These developments are unfolding amid broader concerns about a "new Cold
War" between Western democracies and the "new axis" coalition
[@sanger2024new; @nss2017; @evans2019]. Despite the importance of these issues, 
a lack of systematic quantitative data has limited rigorous investigation. 
Assembling such data is difficult: influencing and target countries rarely publish 
administrative records of influence activity, and less dramatic influence activities 
rarely receive international media attention. This creates a measurement gap 
in the contexts that matter most.

In this paper, we introduce the *Resurgent Authoritarian Influence* (*RAI*) 
dataset. *RAI* tracks monthly reporting across 21 influence categories in `r num_countries` foreign 
aid-receiving low- and middle-income countries from 2012 through August 2025. We 
focus on foreign aid-receiving countries because these are settings where influence 
efforts are often prominent. To build the data, we apply a fine-tuned transformer-based 
language model to a corpus of more than 120 million news articles published by over 350 
high-quality media outlets, most of them domestic, in 40 languages. The result is a
high-frequency measure of reported influence activity by tool and country. *RAI* is a 
media-based measure of reporting intensity, not a record of unique events, but validation 
shows that it strongly correlates with real Russian and Chinese foreign activities.

In addition to introducing *RAI* and its underlying *High-Quality Media from Aid Receiving Countries*
(*HQMARC*) corpus, we provide extensive validation of the data, describe cross-national patterns
in Russian and Chinese activity, and provide a use case examining Russian influence in the months
before the invasion of Ukraine. In doing so, we show that *RAI* is a valuable resource for researchers
and policymakers alike. For researchers, our data provides a complement to existing data on
Chinese financial and diplomatic activities [@goodman2024aiddata; @custer2021tracking], enables
description of how shifts in influence strategies unfold over months and countries, and allows tests
of how influence tools substitute for or complement one another across major geopolitical shocks.
For policymakers, it provides a transparent, updateable gauge of how influence is reported in 
target countries and provides hard data to inform policy responses to the foreign influence of Russia and
China. Throughout, we emphasize that *RAI* measures reporting on influence activity—not verified
actions—and is best interpreted as a high-frequency, multidimensional indicator of salience.

## Russian and Chinese Foreign Influence

Foreign influence, the range of actions governments and state-linked actors take 
to shape the domestic politics, foreign policy preferences, or strategic alignment 
of another state, encompasses both coercive and non-coercive tools, deployed toward 
governments and publics alike [@nye2023rise; @kinne2018defense; @lim2019money]. Which 
tools states choose, toward which targets, and in what sequence are among the central 
questions in international relations research, and ones for which systematic 
cross-national data have been scarce.

Over the past 20 years, Russia and China have increasingly asserted
themselves on the global stage, challenging the liberal international
order and seeking to reshape global dynamics in their favor.
[@sanger2024new; @fukuyama2015end]. Both have increased influence efforts across 
Asia, Africa, Latin America, and Europe---through military interference, investments, 
diplomatic pressure, information campaigns, and cyber operations---while seeking 
to undermine Western influence and secure strategic partnerships with less powerful nations.

Influence strategies are inherently multi-dimensional. States deploy
coercive (e.g., military assistance, sanctions) or non-coercive
tools (e.g., public diplomacy, cultural engagement), targeting elites or
publics depending on objectives and constraints. Changes in influence
behavior thus manifest not only in *how active* states are, but *which tools* 
they emphasize and *where*. A central goal of *RAI* is to make those shifts empirically 
visible. Because influence tools may function as complements or substitutes, tracking 
them together is essential; reporting on Russia's footprint in Africa---where security 
assistance, political engagement, and information operations often blend together---illustrates 
why a multi-dimensional approach is necessary [@ferragamo2023russias; @Gain2023; @Hairsine2023; @Reuters2024].

Despite this policy attention, quantitative data on authoritarian
influence remains sparse. The most comprehensive existing data comes
from AidData, which covers China's foreign aid and state financing to
low- and middle-income countries from 2000–2017 and annual diplomatic
events in some Asian countries [@goodman2024aiddata; @custer2021tracking]. 
This work has generated valuable insights into the effects of Chinese economic 
engagement on conflict, governance, growth, and public opinion [@gehring2019china; @strange2017tracking; @dreher2021aid; @knutsen2020political; @kishi2017chinese; @isaksson2018chinese; @dreher2024aid; @blair2022foreign]. But AidData covers only Chinese influence, is updated sporadically, and
focuses on a limited range of tools. While recent work has begun tracking state-coordinated 
online political influence efforts [@martin2023introducing], research has consequently 
been confined largely to economic influence, leaving diplomacy, hard power, soft power, 
and domestic interference across the full range of bilateral relationships comparatively 
understudied [@nye2023rise; @kurlantzick2007charm; @kinne2018defense].

*RAI* addresses these gaps. It covers both Russia and China and spans 21
influence activities at monthly frequency in 66 countries from 2012 to August 2025. 
Our approach provides unique, high-frequency data
on how Russia and China have wielded their economic and hard power
(military capacity, security agreements, and defense cooperation) to
influence both regional and the international economic order
[@goldstein2020china; @maier1977politics] and pursued overlapping
economic and military cooperation with less powerful nations
[@gowa1993power]. Likewise, we provide systematic data on the use of
soft and diplomatic power [@nye2023rise; @kurlantzick2007charm], i.e.,
non-coercive efforts to shape foreign preferences through public
diplomacy, cultural engagement, and information campaigns. Russia and
China deploy these tools by establishing cultural
centers [@russia_embassy_cambodia_2021] and launching media
campaigns [@cook_ap_2021].
Russia and China also promote their interests using diplomatic
maneuvers, including formal statements, official visits,
and participation in diplomatic mediation [@legarda_merics_2018; @zuvela_vasovic_reuters_2019].
Data tracking the timing and location of soft power and diplomatic
engagement can produce new insights into how and when
non-coercive strategies influence target-country politics, and whether
these tools are used as substitutes or complements to coercive forms of
influence [@ku2022dark; @putnam1988diplomacy; @allan2018distribution].

We also provide data on domestic interference efforts to create
pressure or provide assistance to target governments [@lim2019money]. For Russia and China, this includes everything from surveillance and cyber-attacks [@holland_chiacu_reuters_2021; @bbc_huawei_uganda_zambia_2019; @balkan_n1_cyber_2020; @kafeero_quartz_2020]. We also provide data on the illicit or unintended consequences of influence efforts, including increased corruption and transnational organized crime [@brazys2017bad;
@isaksson2018chinese; @doj_triad_2003]. Data on these adverse types of influence allow research into
the ability of Russia and China to effectively manage their influence
operations. 


## The Resurgent Authoritarian Influence Dataset

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

library(ISOcodes)

# Initialize an empty dataframe to store the results
result_df <- data.frame(country = character(), lsources_len = integer(), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

sum_lengths <- 0
for (i in unique(rai$country)) {
  lsources_len = local_source_select(i)$lsources
  len = length(lsources_len)
  
  # Append the country and the length to the dataframe
  result_df <- rbind(result_df, data.frame(country = i, lsources_len = len))
  
  # Update sum_lengths
  sum_lengths <- sum_lengths + len
}

```

*RAI* tracks *reporting* on 21 influence categories associated with
Russian and Chinese foreign influence. Each category captures reporting
on actions by a government or state-linked actor intended to shape
another country’s domestic or foreign policy. We developed the categories by reviewing prior research and consulting with civil-society and policy partners. We group the 21 categories into six broader themes and
construct theme indices by summing category-level reporting intensities. Table 1 lists the themes, definitions, and categories. See Supplementary Materials *Category Definitions* for category-level definitions.

**Measurement and interpretation.** The classifier assigns category
labels to article text, which we aggregate into monthly reporting
indices. Primary analyses focus on six thematic indices, which are more
stable than fine-grained categories. Some categories intentionally encompass actions with opposite substantive direction (for example, the imposition and removal of sanctions, or the expansion and reduction of diplomatic relations). We classify these together because both represent changes in the use of a common influence instrument. Future research can use the underlying article-level data to distinguish the direction of these activities and examine patterns of escalation, de-escalation, or coercive versus cooperative engagement. We report classifier performance
and training details in the Supplementary Materials. *RAI* measures
*reported* influence activity, not verified actions; covert behaviors
such as intelligence and cyber operations are likely underreported and
should be treated as lower bounds. We mitigate editorial bias by normalizing by 
total article volume, presenting both absolute levels and relative shares, and 
grounding analysis in within-country changes over time.

**The *HQMARC* Corpus.** To measure reported influence activity, we built the 
*High-Quality Media from Aid Receiving Countries* corpus, 
covering `r num_countries` aid-receiving countries from 2012 through
August 2025. *HQMARC* includes over 120 million articles from 16
international outlets, 12 regional outlets, and `r sum_lengths` domestic
newspapers. Domestic sources account for 95% of articles, with a median
of `r median(result_df$lsources_len)` domestic sources per country (see
Supplementary Materials *Distribution of Domestic Sources*). This emphasis on 
domestic media is essential because international outlets provide sparse coverage 
of many countries and typically report only the most salient influence efforts. 
We identify domestic sources using university library guides, Reporters
Sans Frontieres profiles, and partner recommendations. We aim for at least 50%
independent coverage per country, and apply weighting where state-aligned media 
ecosystems dominate (see Supplementary Materials *Source Weighting*). We build custom 
scrapers and parsers for each outlet instead of relying on aggregators such as GDELT, 
Common Crawl, or the Internet Archive. This human-supervised scraping process produces 
a corpus with more stable, well-understood composition [@ml4p2024tracking]. We 
overwhelmingly rely on open-access content. To accommodate diverse languages, 
we translate articles into English before classification; see Supplementary 
Materials *Languages in HQMARC* for details on the translation process and a list of
language coverage by country.^[Given the well-documented biases in English-language 
news sources [@baum2015] even on relatively uncontroversial topics like natural 
disasters [@brimicombe2022], the inclusion of local sources in local languages 
guarantees better coverage. We use neural machine translations (NMT) through Hugging Face or OpenNMT to translate into English. We test the efficacy of all translation models by extracting sample text and running the text through all available translation models on the Hugging Face open database. We then assess whether the translations are sufficient to identify the main influence category being reported on. If they are not, we compare the performances with those of our other APIs and choose the one that yields the optimal sentence-to-sentence translations with sufficient human readability.]


**Classifier.** To classify influence categories, we fine-tuned a ModernBERT-large
classifier on 10,329 human-labeled articles (22 classes including `-999` for articles 
that do not clearly fit any category). We evaluate it with 5-fold cross-validation and 
a held-out test set ($n=1{,}550$). Cross-validation accuracy averages 0.926 with macro F1 of
0.885; held-out test accuracy is 0.923 with macro F1 of 0.883. Performance is strongest 
for high-signal categories (e.g., cyber attack, joint military exercise) and lower 
for linguistically diffuse categories such as diplomatic statements. To ensure articles 
report on actions by China and Russia, we built a keyword library to detect mentions of 
Russian and Chinese agencies, companies, or officials; see Supplementary Material 
*Using Keywords to Detect Influence* for the keyword list and validation. To assign 
articles to target countries, we geoparse the first 600 characters of text; if no 
country is identified, we assign the article to the country of the publishing outlet.^[For international and regional outlets, articles are only assigned to a country if they explicitly mention a location within that country. We use the CLIFF-CLAVIN geoparser with the GeoNames ontological gazetteer. GeoNames is one of the most comprehensive and well-maintained sources of geographic data available, containing over 12 million unique location names across 250 countries [@dignazio2014cliff]. CLIFF API has detailed information on its locations, and we retrieve and convert the country codes of each location to assign the article to a specific location(s). We implement several corrections to the underlying CLIFF system.]

**Aggregation.** We aggregate these data to the country-month level, normalizing 
the count of articles in each influence category by the total number of articles 
published in that country-month. We report *RAI* activity as articles per 10,000 
published, capturing how frequently each category is reported relative to overall 
news volume. We construct theme indices by summing category-specific reporting 
intensities within each theme (Table 1) and supplement them with a surge indicator 
identifying months with unusually large increases in reporting share. Full details 
on model design, parameter tuning, and validation are provided in Supplemental Material. 
Figure 1 shows the data production pipeline.

**Validation.** We conduct two validation exercises. First, we audit change-point months when well-documented episodes should be reflected in *RAI* activity. @fig-sahel-influence plots Russian Hard Power reporting in the three Sahel countries that experienced coups and pivoted from France toward Russia; reporting rises sharply around coup months and remains elevated. @fig-prc-influence shows Chinese Diplomacy reporting in seven countries that switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to the PRC; reporting spikes in each recognition month. These patterns are consistent with well-known shifts in foreign policy alignment. See Supplementary Materials 
*High-Profile Influence Operations* for combined indices.

```{r, fig.width=8,fig.height=4}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| label: fig-sahel-influence
#| fig-cap: "Normalized measure of reporting on Russian Hard Power activities in Sahel countries. Red lines indicate the month of military coups that marked a reorientation away from France and toward Russia."

dat = rai %>%
  filter(influencer == "Russia" & country %in%  c("Mali", "Burkina Faso", "Niger")) 

ggplot(dat, aes(x = date, y =  rai_idx_hp)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .5, color = "black", linetype=1) +
  facet_wrap(~country, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_x_date(breaks = seq(as.Date("2012-01-01"), as.Date(max(rai$date)), by = "6 months"), labels = scales::date_format("%Y-%b"),
              expand = c(.01,.01) ) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 18),  axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust=1),
        axis.title.x = element_blank(),
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 10),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 10)) +
  labs(y = "Russian Hard Power Activity (articles per 10k published)") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = as.Date("2022-01-01")), linetype = "dashed", color = "red", data = dat[dat$country == "Burkina Faso", ]) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = as.Date("2022-09-01")), linetype = "dashed", color = "red", data = dat[dat$country == "Burkina Faso", ]) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = as.Date("2020-08-01")), linetype = "dashed", color = "red", data = dat[dat$country == "Mali", ]) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = as.Date("2021-05-01")), linetype = "dashed", color = "red", data = dat[dat$country == "Mali", ]) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = as.Date("2023-07-01")), linetype = "dashed", color = "red", data = dat[dat$country == "Niger", ])

  facet_wrap(~country, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_x_date(breaks = seq(as.Date("2012-01-01"), as.Date(max(rai$date)), by = "6 months"), labels = scales::date_format("%Y-%b"),
              expand = c(.01,.01) ) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 18),  axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust=1),
        axis.title.x = element_blank(),
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 10),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 8)) +
  labs(y = "Chinese Diplomacy Activity (articles per 10k published)") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = as.Date("2018-05-01")), linetype = "dashed", color = "red", data = dat[dat$country == "Burkina Faso", ]) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = as.Date("2018-05-01")), linetype = "dashed", color = "red", data = dat[dat$country == "Dominican Republic", ]) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = as.Date("2018-08-01")), linetype = "dashed", color = "red", data = dat[dat$country == "El Salvador", ]) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = as.Date("2021-12-01")), linetype = "dashed", color = "red", data = dat[dat$country == "Nicaragua", ]) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = as.Date("2023-03-01")), linetype = "dashed", color = "red", data = dat[dat$country == "Honduras", ]) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = as.Date("2017-06-01")), linetype = "dashed", color = "red", data = dat[dat$country == "Panama", ]) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = as.Date("2019-09-01")), linetype = "dashed", color = "red", data = dat[dat$country == "Solomon Islands", ])
```

Second, we audit 86 randomly selected *RAI* surges encompassing 872 individual articles across 20 event types and 40 countries. Surge detection accurately identified 88 percent (76 of 86). The 10 false positives reflect two systematic limitations (low news volume in some countries and geoparsing errors) discussed fully in Supplementary Materials *Surge Validation*.

**What does *RAI* not measure?** *RAI* captures reporting on influence activity by Russian and Chinese government or state-linked actors; it does not measure influence by non-state actors, third-country governments, or multilateral organizations, and it does not cover advanced democracies or countries outside the 66-country sample. As a media-based measure of reporting intensity, *RAI* does not count discrete events, should not be treated as a census of influence attempts, and measures *reporting* rather than *effectiveness* (i.e., a high score indicates sustained media attention to a type of activity, not that the attempt succeeded).


## Describing Authoritarian Influence Using RAI Data

We characterize RAI activity from 2012 through August 2025 using descriptive analyses only. To account for changes in influence activity associated with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, we distinguish between two periods: 2012–2021 and 2022–2025. Aggregation 
from the monthly level to period averages is performed *after* normalization, 
treating each country-month equally. This ensures that shifts across periods reflect 
broad-based trends rather than a few high-activity months, and hedges against isolated
misclassification errors. For higher-frequency visualizations, see Supplementary 
Materials *Dominant Themes at Higher Frequency*.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

df = read_rai() |>
  filter(! influencer %in% "Combined") |>
  select(country, date, influencer, starts_with("rai_idx"), -rai_idx_total) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("rai_idx"), names_to = "theme") |>
  mutate(theme = gsub("rai\\_idx\\_", "", theme))

df$theme = factor(df$theme)
df$theme = factor(df$theme, levels = gsub("rai_idx_", "", rai_vars_select$variable[2:7]), labels = rai_vars_select$name[2:7])

theme_idx = unique(df$theme)

df = df |>
  group_by(date, influencer, theme) |>
  summarise(value = sum(value) ) |>
  ungroup()

df = df |>
  group_by(influencer, date) |>
  mutate(value = value / sum(value)) |>
  # make it a factor for plotting labels
  mutate(influencer = factor(influencer, levels = c("China", "Russia")))

dip_av = df |>
  filter(theme == "Diplomacy") |>
  mutate(period = case_when(
    date < "2017-01-01" ~ "2012-2016",
    date >= "2017-01-01" & date < "2022-01-01" ~ "2017-2021",
    TRUE ~ "2022-2025"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(period, theme, influencer) |>
  summarise(value = mean(value)) 

cd1 = paste0(round(dip_av[dip_av$influencer == "China" & dip_av$period == "2012-2016",]$value*100, digits=0), "%")
cd2 = paste0(round(dip_av[dip_av$influencer == "China" & dip_av$period == "2017-2021",]$value*100, digits=0), "%")
cd3 = paste0(round(dip_av[dip_av$influencer == "China" & dip_av$period == "2022-2025",]$value*100, digits=0), "%")

rd1 = paste0(round(dip_av[dip_av$influencer == "Russia" & dip_av$period == "2012-2016",]$value*100, digits=0), "%")
rd2 = paste0(round(dip_av[dip_av$influencer == "Russia" & dip_av$period == "2017-2021",]$value*100, digits=0), "%")
rd3 = paste0(round(dip_av[dip_av$influencer == "Russia" & dip_av$period == "2022-2025",]$value*100, digits=0), "%")

```

We begin by identifying the most frequently reported-on theme for each country-period 
(@fig-map_dominant-theme). For China, Economic Power remains the dominant theme across 
countries in both periods, while Diplomacy becomes dominant in a growing subset of cases 
in 2022–2025. Pooling across countries, Diplomacy's share of reported Chinese influence 
rises from `r cd1` (2012–2016) to `r cd2` (2017–2021) to `r cd3` (2022–2025), suggesting 
a gradual rebalancing rather than a wholesale shift away from economic tools.

For Russia, the distribution is more mixed. Diplomacy is frequently dominant, 
but Hard Power becomes more salient in several countries after 2022. Pooling across 
countries, the Diplomacy share rises from `r rd1` (2012–2016) to `r rd2` (2017–2021), 
then falls slightly to to `r rd3` (2022–2025) as Hard Power rises sharply. These patterns 
are consistent with a shift toward more coercive tools after the invasion, though 
they remain measures of reporting rather than direct counts of actions.

@fig-map_russia-influence-share plots Russia's share of total *RAI*
reporting (Russia / \[Russia + China\]), a *relative* measure of the balance of 
reporting between the two actors. Russian activity dominates in parts of Eastern 
and Central Europe and several Sahel countries; Chinese activity is more dominant 
in Southeast Asia and much of Sub-Saharan Africa. In 2022–2025, Russia's share 
increases in the Sahel and North Africa while China retains dominance in Sub-Saharan 
Africa and Southeast Asia. These patterns correspond with widely reported accounts 
of growing Chinese influence in Africa and Latin America during 2012–2021 and more 
recent accounts of increased Russian influence in Africa and Southeast Asia [@ferragamo2023russias;
@kurlantzick2023russias; @gvosdev2016putin], providing face validity for *RAI*.

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Inline-text correlations for the period-change paragraph.
df <- read_rai() |>
  filter(country != "Timor Leste") |>
  select(country, date, rai_idx_total, influencer) |>
  filter(influencer != "Combined")

all_dates <- seq(min(df$date, na.rm = TRUE), rai_end_date, by = "1 month")

df <- df |>
  tidyr::complete(
    country,
    influencer,
    date = all_dates,
    fill = list(rai_idx_total = 0)
  ) |>
  mutate(period = case_when(
    date < "2022-01-01" ~ "2012-2021",
    TRUE ~ "2022-2025"
  )) |>
  select(country, date, rai_idx_total, period, influencer) |>
  group_by(country, period, influencer) |>
  summarize(mean_total_rai = mean(rai_idx_total, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(country, influencer, period)

dfp <- df |>
  group_by(country, influencer) |>
  mutate(
    baseline = lag(mean_total_rai),
    percentage_change = case_when(
      is.na(baseline) ~ NA_real_,
      baseline == 0 & mean_total_rai == 0 ~ 0,
      baseline == 0 & mean_total_rai > 0 ~ 100 * mean_total_rai,
      TRUE ~ (mean_total_rai / baseline - 1) * 100
    )
  )

rc1 <- cor(
  dfp[dfp$period == "2022-2025" & dfp$influencer == "Russia", ]$percentage_change,
  dfp[dfp$period == "2012-2021" & dfp$influencer == "Russia", ]$mean_total_rai,
  use = "complete.obs"
)

dfp_c_share <- dfp |>
  arrange(country, period) |>
  group_by(country, period) |>
  mutate(c_share = mean_total_rai[1] / (mean_total_rai[1] + mean_total_rai[2]))

rc2 <- cor(
  dfp_c_share[dfp_c_share$period == "2022-2025" & dfp_c_share$influencer == "Russia", ]$percentage_change,
  dfp_c_share[dfp_c_share$period == "2012-2021" & dfp_c_share$influencer == "China", ]$c_share,
  use = "complete.obs"
)

rc3 <- cor(
  dfp[dfp$influencer == "Russia", ]$percentage_change,
  dfp[dfp$influencer == "China", ]$percentage_change,
  use = "complete.obs"
)

rc_list <- round(c(rc1, rc2, rc3), 2)

rm(df, dfp, dfp_c_share, rc1, rc2, rc3, all_dates)
```

In summary, the descriptive patterns suggest a rising emphasis on Diplomacy for both Russia and 
China, a post-2022 rise in Russian Hard Power, and continued centrality of Economic 
Power for China, with the two powers targeting largely different countries (cross-country 
correlation in *RAI* changes: `r rc_list[3]`).

## Use Case: Testing Expectations of Russian Influence Activity

To illustrate the analytical value of the RAI data, we examine Russian foreign influence activity in the lead-up to the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine. This case highlights how RAI's high-frequency, multidimensional structure captures patterns of activity that are difficult to observe using existing data sources.

By fall 2021, U.S. intelligence suggests Putin had decided to invade Ukraine [@sanger2024new pp. 237-240]. Knowing that many aid-receiving countries would be pressured by the U.S. and its allies to isolate Russia, we expect that Russia increased foreign influence operations in the preceding months to strengthen diplomatic, military, and economic ties with those countries. The timing of tool choice matters. Soft Power and Domestic Interference operate over the medium term and yield limited immediate material cooperation. Diplomacy, by contrast, can quickly strengthen bilateral relationships, reaffirm existing commitments, and pre-emptively signal consequences for defection — making it well-suited to securing cooperation before an action likely to generate international blowback. High-level Russian diplomatic engagement has been shown to function specifically as a mechanism for deepening bilateral alignment with autocratic target governments [@balci2025giving], consistent with this expectation. Hard Power tools---arms transfers, joint exercises, security agreements---provide immediate material incentives and allow Russia to gain combat experience and test technology before a larger conflict [@goodson2023; @kagan2020]. Importantly, these tools are most valuable when deployed *before* conflict begins; once military activities commence, resources shift to the conflict and the window for influence preparation closes.

To test these expectations, we use change-point detection to identify countries where Russia increased influence operations in the six months before the invasion of Ukraine---the
window when the decision was likely already made [@sanger2024new].
Change-point methods identify the time period with the single largest
level-shift in the mean of a time series [@fryzlewicz2014wild]. We apply
this to each country-theme combination for Russia, recovering the month
when each major level-shift began.
<!-- We investigate the nature and timing of Russian influence operations in the six months before their invasion of Ukraine.  -->

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| label: changepoint-stats

rai_df <- read_rai() %>%
  select(country, influencer, date, rai_idx_bal:rai_idx_sp)

# List of unique country names in your dataframe
unique_countries <- unique(rai_df$country)

result_df <- data.frame()

# Loop through each country
for (country_name in unique_countries) {
  for (j in names(rai_df)[4:9]) {
    # Filter the dataframe for the current country
    dat = rai_df |> filter(country == country_name & influencer == "Russia")

    # Calculate cpt.mean() for the current country
    cpt_result <- cpt.mean(dat[[j]], method = "BinSeg", Q = 1)
    cpt_result = cpt_result@cpts[1]

    country_result <- data.frame(country = country_name, col = j, t(cpt_result))
    result_df <- rbind(result_df, country_result)
  }
}

result_dfi = result_df
for (i in names(result_dfi)[3]) {
  result_dfi[ , i] = NA
  result_dfi[ , i] = as.Date(result_dfi[ , i])

  for (j in 1:nrow(result_dfi)) {
    result_dfi[j , i] = unique(rai_df$date)[result_df[j , i] + 1]
  }
}

dat2 = result_dfi |>
  rename(date = t.cpt_result.,
         theme = col) |>
  group_by(theme, date) |>
  summarise(count = n(), .groups = "drop")

write.csv(dat2, here::here("writing", "output", "change-points_plot.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

pre_start <- as.Date("2021-08-01")
pre_end <- as.Date("2022-01-01")
prev5_start <- as.Date("2016-08-01")
prev5_end <- as.Date("2021-07-01")

cp_counts <- dat2 |>
  filter(date >= pre_start & date <= pre_end) |>
  group_by(theme) |>
  summarise(pre = sum(count), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(
    dat2 |>
      filter(date >= prev5_start & date <= prev5_end) |>
      group_by(theme) |>
      summarise(prev5 = sum(count), .groups = "drop"),
    by = "theme"
  ) |>
  mutate(prev5_avg = prev5 / 10)

get_cp <- function(theme, col) {
  cp_counts[cp_counts$theme == theme, col][[1]]
}

cp_dip_pre <- get_cp("rai_idx_dip", "pre")
cp_dip_prev5 <- get_cp("rai_idx_dip", "prev5")
cp_dip_prev5_avg <- round(get_cp("rai_idx_dip", "prev5_avg"), 1)

cp_hp_pre <- get_cp("rai_idx_hp", "pre")
cp_hp_prev5 <- get_cp("rai_idx_hp", "prev5")
cp_hp_prev5_avg <- round(get_cp("rai_idx_hp", "prev5_avg"), 1)

cp_ep_pre <- get_cp("rai_idx_ep", "pre")
cp_ep_prev5 <- get_cp("rai_idx_ep", "prev5")
cp_ep_prev5_avg <- round(get_cp("rai_idx_ep", "prev5_avg"), 1)

periods <- data.frame(
  start_date = seq.Date(from = as.Date("2012-02-01"), to = as.Date("2021-08-01"), by = "6 months"),
  end_date = seq.Date(from = as.Date("2012-07-31"), to = as.Date("2022-01-31"), by = "6 months")
)

all_combinations <- expand.grid(theme = unique(dat2$theme), period = seq_len(nrow(periods))) |>
  left_join(periods |> mutate(period = seq_len(nrow(periods))) |> select(period, start_date, end_date), by = "period")

period_data <- dat2 |>
  filter(date < as.Date("2022-02-01")) |>
  mutate(period = findInterval(date, periods$start_date, rightmost.closed = TRUE)) |>
  filter(period > 0)

summarized_data <- period_data |>
  group_by(theme, period) |>
  summarise(total_count = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

complete_data <- all_combinations |>
  left_join(summarized_data, by = c("theme", "period")) |>
  mutate(total_count = ifelse(is.na(total_count), 0, total_count))

pre_period_index <- which(periods$start_date == as.Date("2021-08-01"))
complete_data <- complete_data |>
  mutate(pre_invasion = ifelse(period == pre_period_index, 1, 0))

get_p <- function(th) {
  m <- lm(total_count ~ pre_invasion, data = complete_data |> filter(theme == th))
  summary(m)$coefficients["pre_invasion", "Pr(>|t|)"]
}

p_fmt <- function(p) {
  if (is.na(p)) return("p = NA")
  if (p < 0.001) return("p < 0.001")
  sprintf("p = %.3f", p)
}

p_dip <- p_fmt(get_p("rai_idx_dip"))
p_hp <- p_fmt(get_p("rai_idx_hp"))
p_ep <- p_fmt(get_p("rai_idx_ep"))
p_sp <- p_fmt(get_p("rai_idx_sp"))
p_di <- p_fmt(get_p("rai_idx_di"))
```

@fig-changepoint_themes presents evidence broadly consistent with our
expectations. For Diplomacy, Hard Power, and Economic Power, there is a
clear clustering of change-points in the six months before the invasion.
To test this, we count the number of countries with
change-points for each six-month period and regress those counts on an
indicator for the pre-invasion period. Across our six themes, this
indicator is statistically significant for Diplomacy (`r p_dip`) and
Hard Power (`r p_hp`), but not for Economic Power (`r p_ep`), Soft Power
(`r p_sp`), or Domestic Interference (`r p_di`)---consistent with our
expectation that the pre-invasion surge was concentrated in more overt
tools. For Diplomacy, `r cp_dip_pre` countries have change-points in the six
months before the invasion, compared to `r cp_dip_prev5` over the
previous five years (August 2016–July 2021; an average of
`r cp_dip_prev5_avg` change-points per six-month period). For Hard
Power, `r cp_hp_pre` countries have change-points in the immediate
pre-invasion period, compared to `r cp_hp_prev5` over the previous five
years (an average of `r cp_hp_prev5_avg` per six-month period).

#| echo: false

audit_raw <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("code", "validation", "changepoint_gpt", "event_summaries_gpt_summary.csv")
)

audit_pre <- audit_raw |>
  mutate(Date = as.Date(Date, "%m/%d/%Y"),
         Accuracy = ifelse(Signal == "Nothing", "False Positive", "True Positive")) |>
  filter(Date < as.Date("2022-02-01") & Date > as.Date("2021-07-01")) |>
  filter(Event %in% c("Diplomacy", "Hard Power", "Economic Power"))

audit_articles <- sum(audit_pre$Num_Articles, na.rm = TRUE)

audit_summary <- audit_pre |>
  group_by(Event) |>
  summarise(total = n(),
            false_pos = sum(Accuracy == "False Positive"),
            true_pos = sum(Accuracy == "True Positive"),
            .groups = "drop")

get_audit <- function(event, col) {
  audit_summary[audit_summary$Event == event, col][[1]]
}

audit_dip_total <- get_audit("Diplomacy", "total")
audit_dip_false <- get_audit("Diplomacy", "false_pos")

audit_hp_false <- get_audit("Hard Power", "false_pos")

audit_ep_false <- get_audit("Economic Power", "false_pos")

To confirm that these change-points identify substantive real-world developments rather than misclassification, we conduct AI-assisted qualitative analysis. For each country-month in the pre-invasion window (August 2021–January 2022), we pull all relevant articles from *HQMARC* (`r format(audit_articles, big.mark = ",")` articles
total) and prompt GPT-4 to summarize the key developments reported. We then assess whether each change-point reflects genuine Russian influence or misclassification.Change-point months are typically periods of slightly elevated activity *before* the main surge, making this a demanding test of the data's sensitivity to lesser-known episodes. A modest number of misclassifications aside, we find strong evidence that Russia increased diplomatic and military engagement across many countries in the months before the invasion. See Supplementary Materials *Change-point Months in Time-Series* for full details.

We turn next to which countries Russia targeted. IR theory suggests three candidate predictors: ideological proximity to Russia, alignment with mutual partners ("friends of friends" may be easier to persuade [@kinne2018defense]), and economic dependence on Russian exports or imports. We operationalize ideological similarity using UN Ideal Point Distances (UNIPD) [@voetendata]. For each target country, we calculate their average ideal point distance from 2017-2021 with Russia, China, and the Western Powers (U.S., U.K., and France). Similarly, we operationalize economic dependence using COMTRADE data from 2015–2023 (full operationalization details and variable construction appear in Supplementary Materials *Operationalizing Economic Dependence*). Our dependent variable is an indicator for whether a country experienced an RAI influence spike in the six months before the invasion. Table 2 presents OLS results. For each of the three focal *RAI* themes, we run one model with all independent variables excluding UNIPD to China and one model including only UNIPD to China. We run separate models to avoid collinearity between UNIPD partners.^[Our sample includes `r n_strategic` of the `r num_countries` countries in the *RAI* data. We lose `r num_countries - n_strategic` countries from the *RAI* sample due to missing COMTRADE data.]


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

unip_corr <- readr::read_csv(here::here("data", "un_ideal_points_avg.csv")) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(ccode1, country) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(IdealPointDistance = mean(IdealPointDistance, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  dplyr::rename(major_power = country) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = major_power,
                     values_from = IdealPointDistance,
                     names_prefix = "idp_") %>%
  dplyr::rename(idp_UUF = idp_AVG_UKO_FRA_USA)

cor_west_china <- round(cor(unip_corr$idp_UUF, unip_corr$idp_CHN, use = "complete.obs"), 2)
cor_west_russia <- round(cor(unip_corr$idp_UUF, unip_corr$idp_RUS, use = "complete.obs"), 2)
cor_russia_china <- round(cor(unip_corr$idp_RUS, unip_corr$idp_CHN, use = "complete.obs"), 2)
```

The clearest pattern appears in Diplomacy. A one-unit increase in ideological distance from the Western powers ($range = 0.5$–$3.8$) is associated with about a 0.23 decrease in the probability of a Diplomacy change-point, while a one-unit increase in distance from China ($range = 0.08$–$3.1$) is associated with about a 0.32 increase, suggesting Russia's pre-invasion diplomatic outreach focused on countries aligned with the West but relatively distant from China. Hard Power and Economic Power show no consistent ideological or trade-dependence pattern. Given the limited sample (52 countries) and low $R^2$, these results should be read as exploratory: an illustration of the kinds of questions RAI’s multi-dimensional structure enables, not a definitive test.

These patterns may generalize to other cases where a major power anticipates international 
isolation following offensive action, including, potentially, a Chinese military operation 
in Taiwan. *RAI*'s high-frequency, updateable structure makes it possible to monitor for 
analogous pre-crisis surges in near real time. Future research should investigate whether 
pre-emptive influence operations paid off by dissuading targeted countries from complying 
with sanctions or supporting condemnations in international forums.

## Conclusion

The *RAI* dataset provides a multi-dimensional, high-frequency measure of reported 
foreign influence by Russia and China in aid-receiving countries. *RAI* complements 
existing resources---including data on Chinese financial flows [@goodman2024aiddata; @custer2021tracking] 
and conflict-specific external support [@meier2023external]---by extending thematic coverage 
to include diplomacy, hard power, domestic interference, and soft power across all 
countries and time periods in the sample, not only during active conflicts. This breadth 
is a core contribution, even as it comes with narrower geographic scope relative to 
datasets like AidData.

*RAI* is particularly well suited to research on international influence that has been constrained by limited data on the timing and composition of influence activities. Rather than recording only whether influence occurred, *RAI* tracks multiple instruments of state influence at monthly frequency, allowing researchers to examine how influence strategies evolve over time. This temporal resolution makes it possible to study when and how states seek cooperation or control [@kinne2018defense; @lake1996anarchy], whether diplomatic, military, informational, and economic tools substitute for or complement one another [@ku2022dark; @putnam1988diplomacy], and how influence strategies adapt to short-term geopolitical shocks. Because RAI follows both Russia and China within the same country-month panel, it also enables researchers to test whether the two powers compete, specialize, or coordinate across recipient countries [@sanger2024new], moving beyond descriptive comparisons to evaluate strategic interaction over time.

*RAI* is equally valuable for research on conflict and domestic politics. Its high-frequency measurement allows researchers to study how influence activities are sequenced before, during, and after international crises, militarized disputes, coups, or contested elections. For example, merging *RAI* with UN General Assembly voting records [@voetendata] makes it possible to test whether Russian diplomatic and military engagement before the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine influenced states' voting behavior during the subsequent emergency General Assembly sessions. The Domestic Interference category likewise facilitates research on authoritarian promotion and democratic backsliding [@diamond2020democratic; @balci2025giving], while combining RAI with data on Chinese development finance [@goodman2024aiddata] enables tests of how economic and political influence reinforce one another. More generally, RAI provides a foundation for studying not only whether states exert influence, but also how influence strategies evolve across time, policy domains, and geopolitical contexts.

The data have important limitations. *RAI* is media-based and reflects reporting salience 
rather than verified action counts, covert activities should be treated as lower bounds, 
and cross-country level comparisons warrant caution given variation in media capacity 
and press freedom. Lastly, automated classification introduces some error (as in the case 
with human classification), particularly for complex or multi-topic articles.

In sum, *RAI* advances our ability to track authoritarian influence at high frequency 
and across multiple tools. As great power competition intensifies, such data will be 
vital for scholars testing theories of tool substitution and strategic sequencing, and 
for policymakers seeking transparent, updateable assessments of how influence is reported in 
target-country media. *RAI* is distributed as a country-month panel upon request, 
but researchers may request data at alternative levels of temporal aggregation (e.g., weekly) 
to match the needs of different research designs and theoretical expectations about how 
influence is sequenced over time. Our infrastructure is designed for quarterly updates 
and expansion to additional actors and categories as the geopolitical landscape evolves.

Furthermore, this dataset can aid policymakers in crafting diplomatic and strategic approaches that align with ever-changing geopolitical realities, enhancing the ability to anticipate or mitigate the influence exerted by these countries.
